data.title: Democrats must tackle affordability without breaking the budget
data.description:
After posting the most sweeping victory in the midterm elections since Watergate, the looming issue for Democrats is what they should do to retain control of Congress and win the presidency in 2028.  

A key factor behind the landslide win was voter concerns about the high cost of living, which Democrats linked to Trump’s actions on tariffs, the war with Iran that boosted gas and diesel prices and cutbacks in benefits that will raise healthcare costs for many Americans. They now need to reverse these actions by using the power of the purse they will have. 

One challenge they will face is a veto by Trump on legislation that requires two-thirds of both Houses of Congress to override. Another is they are divided between centrists who are willing to compromise to enact legislation and progressives who want to expand social programs through increased government spending. 

So how should Democrats proceed? 

In a prior commentary, I argued that Congress should begin by reasserting its control over trade policy. The starting point should be to renew the United States-Mexico-Canada trade agreement that President Trump suspended. The actions that he took to boost tariffs on Canadian goods were highly unpopular in states that bordered Canada and throughout the Midwest. Consequently, there is bipartisan support to renew the USMCA, and Congress should follow by considering ways to lower tariffs in Europe and Asia. 

Congress should also use its power to pressure President Trump to wind down the war with Iran. Trump is pressing Senate Republicans to pass $350 billion in defense spending through a party line vote in the current congressional session. However, press reports indicate that Republican leaders will first attempt to negotiate a deal with Democrats. This reflects their awareness of how unpopular the Iran war is and concerns about the budgetary impact. 

Democrats should also press to overturn legislative cuts of over $1 trillion over a 10-year period for programs such as Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act. The cutbacks are projected to leave an estimated 10 million to 16 million people uninsured by 2034 and will boost costs of those who are insured. Even if Democrats are unable to override a presidential veto, it would signal to voters what they are prepared to do should they win the presidency in 2028. 

What mistakes should Democrats avoid? 

The biggest would be for them to believe voters have given them a lasting mandate.  When Joe Biden won the presidency in November 2020, it was expected he would govern from the center. However, Biden tacked to the left when the Democrats gained control of Congress, and he embarked on the biggest government programs since Lyndon Baines Johnson’s Great Society. 

An analysis by Brookings of Biden’s fiscal legacy sheds light on why most voters were not enamored with “Bidenomics.” The report acknowledges that Biden inherited a challenging fiscal situation due to the COVID-19 pandemic, but he subsequently enacted a wish list of new spending initiatives that tallied $6.6 trillion over a 10-year period. Democrats need to acknowledge that they cannot go on another spending spree. If they did, it would inevitably spur higher inflation as it did in 2021-2022. 

The backdrop is that Washington’s budget binge over the past 25 years has driven government debt held by the public from 32 percent to 100 percent of GDP, and it is poised to climb higher. Ongoing budget deficits of 6 percent of GDP are not sustainable. 

Meanwhile, the bipartisan refusal to address Social Security and Medicare shortfalls has closed several options for reforming these programs. The cash shortfall of the two programs is projected to result in a significant decline in the respective reserve balances in the years ahead that could affect their viability. There is no plausible package other than tax increases or spending savings that can offset this shortfall.  

So, what might be done to improve the fiscal outlook? 

Democrats should start by aiming to revamp Trump’s signature legislation, the “One Big Beautiful Bill.” It is the most regressive legislation since the progressive income tax was introduced in 1914. The tax cuts and cutbacks in benefits widened the income disparities between the poor and middle- income households and the very rich.   

At the same time, Democrats must recognize that broad-based tax increases are highly unpopular with voters. Rather, the goal should be to achieve tax reform. The template could be the Tax Reform Act of 1986 that was designed to simplify the income tax code, broaden the tax base and eliminate many tax shelters. It passed with bipartisan support, but many of the loopholes that disappeared then are back along with new ones. 

Finally, while both Democrats and Republicans cater to their respective bases today, they cannot ignore independent voters who now tally 45 percent of the electorate and increasingly dictate the outcome of national elections. 

Nicholas Sargen, Ph.D., is affiliated with the Darden Business School. He has authored three books including “Investing in the Trump Era.”

data.title: Mamdani on crutches after tearing Achilles in soccer match against media team
data.description:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is on crutches after he tore his Achilles tendon playing soccer, the mayor said Friday. 

Mamdani appeared injured at a Friday morning press conference before disclosing the injury he said occurred during a soccer game against the city press corps. A longtime fan and competitive soccer player up until his mayoral run, Mamdani said he didn’t stretch before playing and will be in a boot for six to eight weeks. 

“I scored a goal soon after getting on the pitch and I forgot that I was 35,” Mamdani said, “And soon after I tore my Achilles.” 

The mayor grew up playing soccer in New York City and continued to play on a recreational team called the ‘Talking Headers’ up until the launch of his 2025 mayoral campaign. Mamdani, who was announcing the planned closure of the notorious New York City jail on Rikers Island, said he will play soccer again in nine months. 

“It is an honor to stand, barely, alongside New Yorkers who have spent decades devoting themselves to a vision of our city that many said was impossible,” Mamdani joked as he kicked off his speech.

The mayor reportedly arrived to the pickup soccer game late and said he did not stretch before hitting the field. Mamdani said his team won the game 10-5.

data.title: Watch live: Trump briefs on Asia trip after Xi, Putin summit
data.description:
President Trump will brief reporters Friday on his high-profile trip to Asia, which included an unprecedented trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Trump is expected to tout trade agreements reached with Thailand and the Philippines, as well as a symbolic peace declaration issued alongside Xi and Putin. The summit, which garnered some scrutiny, appeared to produce few concrete breakthroughs.

The president was also expected to discuss rapidly advancing artificial intelligence with his Chinese counterpart during the visit. Concerns over AI and cybersecurity have intensified over the past week following a series of widespread technology outages.

The White House briefing is scheduled to begin at noon EST.

Watch the live video above.

data.title: Bessent says Jensen Huang did not come up during China discussions
data.description:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was not a topic of discussion between U.S. and Chinese officials during a summit in China this week.

When CNBC’s Sara Eisen asked the Treasury secretary whether the tech mogul came up in conversations, he replied, “No.”

President Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Asia Pacific Economic Forum (APEC) this week, days after Huang departed Nvidia amid reports about his extramarital affairs — including one with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang.

Jensen Huang had successfully lobbied the Trump administration to ease export controls on Nvidia’s chips, allowing the company to sell them to China. 

Bessent said Friday that Nvidia’s H200 chips are the “threshold level” of chips the firm can sell to China.

“That continues as planned and … everything beneath there,” the Treasury secretary added on “Squawk Box.”

In the wake of Jensen Huang’s resignation, Nvidia’s board of directors formed a committee to oversee export controls. The committee will receive legal, national security and trade compliance advice from outside experts, the company noted in a Tuesday release.

Bessent, though, said he does not “anticipate” a change in the administration’s policy regarding export controls on Nvidia’s chips.

“President Trump was very clear when he made the policy. He drew a very firm line at the H200s, and believes that is the level that China should be able to get.”

Trump, who has backed Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, told Fox News on Wednesday he “might have” brought up the situation “briefly” with Xi.

“It’s such a tragedy,” he told Jacqui Heinrich, calling Jensen Huang a “brilliant man.”

data.title: Russian 'comfortable' with NATO-style security guarantee for Ukraine, Kushner says
data.description:
Russia is open to Ukraine having a mutual defense pact with the U.S. and European countries, similar to NATO’s Article 5 commitment, President Trump’s son-in-law and top envoy for negotiations between Russia and Ukraine said on Thursday. 

Speaking after a multinational gathering of Ukraine’s supporters, Jared Kushner said the Russians are open to accepting Ukraine maintaining robust security guarantees, despite Moscow pointing to NATO enlargement as one of the triggers for its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February of 2022. 

“I think we’ve gotten the Russians comfortable with that concept, where any security guarantee for Ukraine would be based on Article 5,” Kushner said at a press conference in Berlin, alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, and some of Ukraine’s most prominent European partners, including Germany, France, and the United Kingdom. 

“I think that that comes with at least, what the Russians are saying, the intention is, when this war is over, to not have another war in the future.”

Kushner said he understands there’s “a lot of skepticism and disbelief” on Russia holding to that position, but said it’s important to start dialogue between Europe and the Kremlin. 

“Let people discuss it. Let them hear it from each other.”

Zelensky said that the best security guarantee for Ukraine, and Europe as a whole, is NATO membership. 

“NATO and the EU have been and will remain the pillars of the European security architecture,” he said during the press conference.

“And we all understand that with Ukrainian strength, Ukrainian experience, and Ukrainian technologies, NATO and the EU will be far more reliable defenders of the European way of life and European security.”

The press conference happened shortly after Trump called into the meeting after he held his own meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China. Trump met privately with Putin, and in an unprecedented trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Trump said in his call that Putin is serious about negotiating a peace deal with Ukraine, Politico reported.

Meanwhile, attacks continued overnight, with Ukraine targeting Russia’s Kerch bridge for the third time in three days. The massive road and rail bridge connects Russia with the occupied Crimean peninsula and is a symbol of Putin’s commitment to hold onto the territory since Russia annexed it in 2014. Ukraine’s military succeeded in damaging a portion of the bridge’s road in a major attack.

Russian attacks on Ukraine overnight between Thursday to Friday included at least 98 drones and an unspecified number of Onyx anti-ship missiles, a supersonic cruise missile which has a range of nearly 200 miles, according to an analysis by the Institute for the Study of War.

Russia is escalating its attacks against Ukrainian energy infrastructure and civilian targets across the country. 

The European Union Ambassador to Ukraine, Katarina Mathernova, posted on X that Russia was attacking Kyiv “relentlessly” on Thursday, with dozens of air raid sirens and narrowly escaping a drone explosion above her head as she ran into a hotel. She said the Dutch embassy and three other embassies have sustained damage in the attacks. 

“There’s nowhere to hide from this war. russians attack everywhere. This is what Ukrainians have lived with for five years. I believe Ukraine will hold out, as it has done so far, and in the end it will prevail,” she wrote on X.

data.title: Live updates: Trump briefs reporters on China summit; GOP at odds over reconciliation
data.description:
President Trump, fresh from his trip to Asia, is set to brief reporters on his trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Trump touted the rare summit as “Great and Highly Consequential” in a post online following the meeting. Earlier Thursday, the trio announced the talks yielded a symbolic “declaration toward peace.”

Meanwhile, Senate Republicans are increasingly at odds over the Trump administration’s push for a $350 billion Pentagon funding package. Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) warned that the reconciliation process could expose deep divisions within the GOP over Medicaid cuts enacted last year.

Some lawmakers are eager to revisit the healthcare reductions, while others fear reopening the debate could unravel key provisions of Trump’s signature tax law. Hill Insiders can learn more here.

On Thursday, Senate Republicans blocked another war powers resolution that would restrict further military operations in Iran. The upper chamber did advance the bipartisan permitting reform bill though, sending it to the House.

A federal district court in Virginia will also hear arguments Friday on a lawsuit seeking to prevent the construction of Trump’s proposed 250-foot triumphal arch. The hearing comes two days after a federal judge extended the block on construction.

Trump will host a reception in the afternoon and hold signing time. First lady Melania Trump, whose docuseries premiered late Thursday on Prime Video, will attend an arrival ceremony for the White House Christmas tree.

Follow live below.

data.title: Democrats press Lutnick for Megaspeed investigation findings
data.description:
Reps. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-Calif.) and Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), ranking member on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, are pressing Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for information about the agency’s investigation into Megaspeed.

Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company, is facing a probe from the Department of Commerce and Department of Justice (DOJ) over whether it helped smuggle advanced AI chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls.

But Commerce’s role in the investigation has come under scrutiny after The New York Times reported that Nvidia’s general counsel Tim Teter reached out to agents working on the case last year.

Teter reportedly said Under Secretary of Commerce Jeff Kessler had given the company permission to reach out. Kessler heads up the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), which oversees export controls.

“The American public and Congress deserve a full accounting of what happened,” Kamlager-Dove and Meeks wrote in a letter to Lutnick on Thursday.

The case was transferred to the DOJ shortly after Teter’s outreach, according to The Times. The agencies said in a joint statement Monday that the Justice Department “took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed” following an on-site inspection of the company last June.

The lawmakers called for answers as to “whether Under Secretary Kessler permitted or encouraged Nvidia to contact BIS agents actively investigating transactions in which the company was involved, and whether the Department allowed a major American corporation that is financially and personally linked to the Trump Administration to interfere with law enforcement activity.”

They are seeking information about when BIS launched its investigation into Megaspeed, what information was gathered, whether the probe was halted, what communications Kessler had with Nvidia about Megaspeed and whether Nvidia received any nonpublic information.

“The Department of Commerce has a responsibility to protect American national security, enforce export control laws, and ensure that no corporation receives preferential treatment in matters involving potential violations of federal law,” they added.

data.title: These 14 Democratic senators voted to loosen environmental laws to speed up energy buildout
data.description:
The Senate voted late Thursday night to pass a law that seeks to speed up the nation’s energy and infrastructure buildout, including by loosening its environmental laws.

The bill was a bipartisan push, spearheaded by Democrats Sheldon Whitehouse (R.I.) and Martin Heinrich (N.M.) alongside Republicans Shelley Moore Capito (W.Va.) and Mike Lee (Utah).

Nevertheless, most Democrats opposed the law, citing among their concerns its loosening of environmental laws, lessening of tribal input into projects that may impact them and potential to bolster fossil fuel production and infrastructure.

The bill particularly makes changes to the Clean Water Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the Endangered Species Act.

This includes language that makes it harder for the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and states to block projects on environmental grounds.

It also includes language exempting certain activities, including expansions to natural gas pipelines; makes it more difficult for opponents of a project to sue over it; extends how long water quality permits can last before they need to be renewed; and adds hurdles to the EPA’s ability to set water quality criteria. 

It also changes the Endangered Species Act, including a change to the definition of “best available science” that’s required to be used to determine whether a species should get legal protections — in a way that environmentalists say creates a high threshold for protections. 

These fourteen Democrats voted for it: Whitehouse, Heinrich, Chris Coons (Del.), John Fetterman (Pa.), Ruben Gallego (Ariz.), John Hickenlooper (Colo.), Amy Klobuchar (Minn.), Gary Peters (Mich.), Jack Reed (R.I.), Jacky Rosen (Nev.), Brian Schatz (Hawaii), Chuck Schumer (N.Y.), Elissa Slotkin (Mich.) and Mark Warner (Va.). Also among the yes votes was Angus King (I-Maine), who caucuses with Democrats.

The bill also contains significant wins for Democrats on climate and renewable energy — and the bill’s Democratic supporters point to analyses showing that it’s actually projected to bring down U.S. emissions.

Among the key provisions expected to bolster solar and wind power is a new authority granted to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission allowing it to approve new powerlines when states don’t do so, which is expected to help get more renewable power onto the grid. 

It also contains provisions that would force data centers to pay for any electricity cost increases their demand would cause. Supporters have pointed to one analysis saying the bill will save consumers $50 to $78 per year on their electric bills in 2040.

Whitehouse and Heinrich have been championing the legislation calling it a win for the climate as well as affordability. 

“The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will get more affordable energy onto the grid faster, make data centers pay their fair share of electricity and grid costs, and create more than 100,000 good-paying American jobs — all while maintaining important environmental protections and strengthening Tribal consultation,” Heinrich said in a statement on the legislation. 

“This bill kicks off Democrats bringing down energy costs, lowering emissions, creating well-paying jobs, and ending the free ride for data centers,” Whitehouse said in his own statement. “Americans will quickly begin getting some relief on their energy bills if the House follows suit.”

Other Democratic and Democratic-caucusing supporters seemed torn. In a statement shared with The Hill, King said that his vote “wasn’t an easy choice.”

“I listened to my environmental friends in Maine, many of whom were opposed to the bill, I talked to people in the energy field, particularly in the renewable field, and decided that on balance this bill is a lot better than the status quo,” King said. 

“This bill unlocks an enormous amount of renewable energy, that is now basically unable to get to the market because of a lack of transmission,” he added.

data.title: Stock investors are giving up on China
data.description:
China’s closely watched CSI 300 Index has fallen 20 percent from June highs and is now officially in bear-market territory.  

Chinese stocks have lost more than $3.5 trillion in value since the middle of the year. Many analysts believe that shares are still on a downward path. Morgan Stanley, for instance, sees perhaps another 15 percent drop.

“If the country is winning the future, why are its investors so glum?” asks the Economist in an article titled “China’s Stock Markets Are the Great Global Exception.” The S&P 500 in the U.S. has gained 53 percent over the last five years. In Europe, the FTSE 500 has gained 45 percent. The CSI 300 has now lost 18.5 percent in the same period.

Chinese stocks are hitting lows for two fundamental reasons. For one thing, Xi Jinping’s economic plans are not working. Second, Xi is adopting policies that reduce or even eliminate profits at listed companies, scaring away investors — especially domestic investors.  

On the first point, the Chinese economy, especially from the outside, looks bright and shiny because of the country’s leadership in a number of crucial technology areas. Xi’s Made in China 2025 initiative and five-year plans — China is now in the first year of its 15th five-year plan — along with associated programs, are all tech-heavy.

“The country’s technology companies are forging ahead,” Andrew Collier, a research fellow at the Harvard Kennedy School’s Mossavar-Rahmani Center, told me this month. He noted that corporate profits for high technology manufacturing rose 52 percent in the first nine months of this year. However, such manufacturing only accounts for roughly 6 percent of the country’s economy.

Optimists point out that the export sector is another success story. The country’s trade surplus at the end of October hit a stunning $1.04 trillion. But paradoxically, many export-oriented factories are earning only thin margins and are not doing well. This appears to be the reason why the central government, through brazen currency interventions, is slowing the rise of the renminbi. The manipulation is of course attracting criticism from the country’s trading partners.

The rest of the economy is deteriorating fast. The property sector at the end of last decade accounted for about a quarter of gross domestic product. Now, the extreme oversupply — the country has more vacant housing than its entire population of 1.4 billion people could fill — is weighing heavily on growth.

With housing prices falling, a negative wealth effect is weighing on consumption. Furthermore, Xi’s relentless drive for automation, which is producing the world’s most advanced robots, is aggravating both unemployment and underemployment.

Urban unemployment, officially pegged at 5.2 percent in September, is probably closer to 20 percent overall and much higher for the crucial 16 to 24 age cohort. Some recent college graduates are not even looking for white-collar jobs, heading straight to menial employment out of school. Gig jobs employ a stunning 44 percent of the country’s workforce. 

Consumption in China accounts for only about 38 percent of GDP, one of the lowest consumption-contribution rates in the world. And from all indications consumption’s role is continuing to decline.

The central government has sporadically introduced measures to stimulate consumer spending, but they are almost always one-off programs that have no lasting effect. Xi has not implemented structural reforms that will empower consumers at the expense of state enterprises and state banks.

In sum, GDP growth, in reality, is almost certainly less than the 4.5 percent reported for the third quarter of this year. 

“China’s split economy — booming in tech and slowing in everything else — is coming apart,” says economic analyst Andrew Collier.

Second, domestic investors realize that Xi is trying to take away almost all of the benefits of the country’s tech wonders. For instance, he is commoditizing China’s tech products so that they flood the world. This process, however, reduces corporate profits and therefore investor interest. 

Take the initial public offering of CXMT on July 27. The memory chip firm became the most valuable Chinese public company on its first day of trading. But as Alicia Garcia-Herrero of The Wire China wrote, investors viewed the company as just “another heavily subsidized entrant” that “would now be racing to add capacity into a market already braced for a price war.”  

Investors know by now that they do not control company decisions; Xi does. And he has very different goals than they have. It does not help, as Collier noted, that the “Nvidia blow-up” and related concerns “have scared away some investors in the artificial intelligence boom.”

Because of these fundamental problems, the Chinese government’s support measures have not been particularly effective this year. China’s officials every so often mount a rescue operation by the so-called “national team,” as they did in the middle of July when state-controlled firms went into the market to buy $8.9 billion of shares. But investors this year have been ignoring the government’s desire that they buy stocks.

Earlier this month, the government banned initial public offerings and large stock sales. As the Wall Street Journal’s Lingling Wei wrote, “Intervention looks more like a Band-Aid than a cure.” 

Nothing seems to be working to keep stock prices high, and nothing will work until Xi stops trying to command the economy and the markets.

Gordon G. Chang is the author of “Plan Red: China’s Project to Destroy America” and “The Coming Collapse of China.”

data.title: Boyle says Fetterman 'would probably finish last' in a 2028 Democratic primary
data.description:
Rep. Brendan Boyle (D-Pa.) said Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) would likely “finish last” in the Democratic primary if he runs for reelection in 2028.

“I think this coffee table could beat John Fetterman in the Democratic primary,” Boyle told Punchbowl News. “If he were to run and it was a five, six-way race, he would probably finish last.”

Fetterman recently hinted at running for reelection in 2028, saying he is “considering things.”

When asked if he is worried about a primary challenger in 2028, Fetterman pointed to Boyle.

“You have the little guy from Philly. You can ask him why he chickened out,” he said.

The House Democrat said he does not plan to challenge Fetterman, instead choosing to remain in the lower chamber where he is in line to be the next chair of the House Budget Committee.

Fetterman recently suggested that could leave the party if Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) is elected as the Senate majority leader, calling it troubling if his “caucus elects someone like Van Hollen that has really made his name being” hostile to Israel. A poll earlier in August showed Fetterman was more popular among Pennsylvania Republicans than Democrats. 

As Fetterman is considering a reelection bid in 2028, multiple candidates are lining up to possibly challenge him for his Senate seat.

Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.) said he is seriously considering a 2028 primary challenge against the incumbent, saying, “Fetterman’s been a mess and he doesn’t take the job seriously. Whatever I decide to do, that guy is not going to be the senator in ’28.”

Less than a week after the midterm elections, Ahmed Moor, a Palestinian American writer, businessperson and a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, announced a Senate bid against Fetterman.

“I’m running to end the war in Iran and to promote the dignity agenda: free healthcare, free childcare, and affordable housing,” Moor wrote on the social platform X.

A day after Moor’s announcement, Rep. Madeleine Dean (D-Pa.) also said she is considering challenging Fetterman, saying, “I have been concerned about, really, two things, which is his family and his health … and am very disappointed in his activity as a senator and in his votes.”
